name: TB-500

b.x: Seven amino acids. That is all TB-500 is. Acetylated leucine-lysine-lysine-threonine-glutamate-threonine-glutamine, pulled from positions 17 through 23 of the 43-amino-acid thymosin beta-4 protein. CAS number 885340-08-9, molecular weight 889.0 Da. The mechanism is well characterized in animals. TB-500 binds monomeric G-actin, sequestering free actin subunits and remodeling the cytoskeleton so that endothelial and immune cells migrate faster to damaged tissue. It upregulates VEGF 2.5 to 3.8-fold. Malinda and colleagues confirmed that thymosin beta-4 increased reepithelialization by 42% at day 4 and 61% at day 7 versus controls in rat full-thickness skin wounds [1]. It also suppresses myofibroblast differentiation, which reduces scar formation. What makes TB-500 unusual is systemic distribution. You don't need to inject near the injury. Subcutaneous injection in the abdomen reaches a torn rotator cuff the same way it reaches a strained hamstring. Community users have validated this property thousands of times over. No published study has given the TB-500 fragment to people. FDA's briefing for the July 2026 compounding advisory committee meeting found no clinical studies or human exposure data for it by any route. A 2024 metabolite study by Rahaman and colleagues added a wrinkle: the parent compound showed no wound-healing activity in vitro. The metabolite Ac-LKKTE was the active species. That finding has not changed community dosing practices, but it raises questions about mechanism attribution. Community confidence (4.1/5 sentiment, 500+ r/Peptides threads) sits well ahead of the formal evidence base. TB-500 was on the FDA Category 2 list from 2024 until its nominators withdrew it; FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists it as withdrawn. PCAC discussed it on July 23, 2026. No FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list, so compounding pharmacies cannot use it today. All current supply is unregulated gray-market product.

TB-500 works through actin dynamics. The peptide binds to monomeric G-actin and sequesters free actin subunits, shifting the balance of cytoskeletal assembly inside cells. When cells need to migrate to an injury site, they depend on rapid actin polymerization at the leading edge. TB-500 regulates that process. This actin-sequestering activity drives two downstream effects. The first is angiogenesis. TB-500 upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) 2.5 to 3.8-fold in preclinical models. More capillaries at the injury site mean better oxygen delivery and faster tissue remodeling. The second downstream effect is anti-fibrotic. TB-500 inhibits myofibroblast differentiation, the process responsible for excessive scar tissue formation. In preclinical wound models, this translated to cleaner healing with less fibrosis. Malinda and colleagues published the foundational wound healing data in 1999 [1]. Thymosin beta-4 increased reepithelialization by 42% at day 4 and 61% at day 7 versus controls. Bock-Marquette and colleagues confirmed cardioprotective effects after myocardial infarction in animal models [3]. A 2026 review in Cureus (PMC12753158) placed TB-500 among the most promising orthopedic peptides based on preclinical data quality. One important caveat: a 2024 metabolite study found that the TB-500 parent compound had no wound-healing activity in vitro. The metabolite Ac-LKKTE was the active species. In-vivo activity may depend on metabolic conversion.
TB-500 benefits center on systemic tissue repair, angiogenesis, and anti-fibrotic activity.

Systemic healing without site-specific injection. TB-500 distributes throughout the body after subcutaneous injection. Community users consistently confirm that injection location does not affect results for distant injuries.
Angiogenesis with VEGF upregulation of 2.5 to 3.8-fold in preclinical models. New capillary formation at injury sites improves oxygen and nutrient delivery during repair.
Anti-fibrotic activity through myofibroblast suppression. TB-500 reduces scar tissue formation during healing, which translates to better tissue quality and flexibility in recovered areas.
Soft tissue recovery for tendons, ligaments, and muscle tears. Community reports across 500+ threads consistently describe pain reduction and improved range of motion by weeks 3 to 4 of loading.

Paired with BPC-157 in the "Wolverine Stack," the most popular healing combination in the peptide community. BPC-157 handles local repair near the injection site; TB-500 provides systemic angiogenic support. In a 2026 rat Achilles study [4], TB-500 alone improved tendon strength, and adding BPC-157 gave no extra benefit.
Partially Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 12 key studies · Preclinical
Strong preclinical evidence for thymosin beta-4 and its active fragment in wound healing, angiogenesis (VEGF upregulation 2.5–3.8×), and actin-mediated cell migration.

Dosing studied: 4–5 mg/week (2–2.5 mg 2×/week) loading for 4–6 weeks; maintenance at 1,000-2,000 mcg once weekly (community reports): derived entirely from community consensus extrapolated from preclinical data; no human dose-finding study completed for the TB-500 fragment specifically

Fragment-specific human data is absent: both published phase 1 trials, Ruff 2010 [5] and Wang 2021 [2], used full 43-AA thymosin beta-4, not the 7-AA TB-500 fragment. A 2024 metabolite study (Rahaman et al., J Chromatogr B) found the TB-500 parent compound had no wound-healing activity in vitro: metabolite Ac-LKKTE was the active species, introducing uncertainty about in vivo mechanism attribution. FDA's briefing for the July 2026 PCAC meeting found no clinical studies or human exposure data for TB-500 by any route.
Key Study

Malinda et al. 1999, "Thymosin beta 4 accelerates wound healing," J Invest Dermatol. PMID 10469335: full TB4 increased reepithelialization 42% at day 4 and 61% at day 7 vs. controls in rat full-thickness skin wounds; foundational study establishing the wound healing mechanistic basis (note: tested full TB4, not TB-500 fragment)
Limitations

No human trial of the TB-500 fragment has been published at any phase. Two published IV phase 1 trials, Ruff 2010 (PMID 20536472) and Wang 2021 (PMID 34346165), tested the full parent protein, 43-AA thymosin beta-4: PK and safety data cannot be directly applied to the 7-AA fragment. 2024 metabolite study suggests the parent peptide may be inactive in vitro; in-vivo activity may depend on metabolic conversion to Ac-LKKTE. No published human PK characterization for TB-500 fragment. Long-term safety unknown. Theoretical oncogenic risk from pro-angiogenic mechanism is unresolved. No rodent-validated human dose range.
Community Experience
One of the most trusted healing peptides in the research community (4.1/5 sentiment, 500+ r/Peptides threads).

Community dosing: 4–5 mg/week loading (2–2.5 mg 2×/week for 4–6 weeks), then maintenance at 1,000-2,000 mcg once weekly (community reports); conservative start: 2 mg 2×/week; aggressive acute injury: up to 10 mg/week for 2–4 weeks maximum

Standard loading/maintenance structure is well-established and consistently reproduced across community reports. Most valued for tendon, ligament, and muscle injury recovery. Key advantage repeatedly cited: systemic action means no need to inject at the injury site. Main concerns are cost and sourcing quality variability under current FDA restrictions.

Community protocols are consistent with the preclinical mechanistic data (angiogenesis, actin sequestration, systemic distribution). However, the 2024 metabolite study challenges direct attribution of wound-healing activity to the parent peptide, and no human RCT for the fragment exists. Community confidence significantly exceeds what the fragment-specific evidence base strictly supports. The systemic dosing approach (injection site irrelevance) is mechanistically well-grounded.
Community Community dosing consensus from peptide research communities

All TB-500 dosing is community-driven. No human dose-finding study exists for the fragment. Beginner: 2000 mcg (2 mg) twice weekly. Moderate: 2500 mcg (2.5 mg) twice weekly. Aggressive: 5000 mcg (5 mg) twice weekly. Reconstitution math for a 5 mg vial with 1 mL bacteriostatic water: concentration is 5000 mcg per mL. Each 10 units on a 100-unit insulin syringe equals 500 mcg. So 2000 mcg (beginner dose) is 40 units. For a 10 mg vial with 1 mL BAC water: 10,000 mcg per mL, meaning 20 units for 2000 mcg. The loading phase matters more than anything else. Skipping it is the single most common reason for disappointing results. You need 2 injections per week for at least 4 to 6 weeks to build adequate tissue-level concentrations. Going straight to once-weekly maintenance is an underdose. Don't train through the injury during a TB-500 protocol. The community figured this out quickly: TB-500 accelerates repair, but it doesn't protect against re-injury from continued loading of the damaged tissue. Relative rest of the injured structure speeds outcomes. Injection site does not need to be near the injury. Abdomen or thigh, alternating sides.

Loading phase: full dose 2x/week for 4-6 weeks. Then maintenance: 1,000-2,000 mcg once weekly (community reports). Repeat loading if needed for new injuries.

Avoid
Anti-VEGF therapies (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept)
TB-500 upregulates VEGF 2.5–3.8-fold. Anti-VEGF agents directly antagonize this mechanism. Concurrent use creates direct pharmacodynamic opposition and defeats the purpose of TB-500.
High-dose chronic NSAIDs

Chronic high-dose NSAIDs may blunt TB-500 angiogenic signaling through prostaglandin pathway suppression. Short-term/low-dose NSAID use for acute pain management is unlikely to be clinically significant.
Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs)
TB-500 promotes angiogenesis at healing sites. Concurrent anticoagulation may increase bleeding risk at sites of active new vascular formation.
Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate)
TB-500 modulates immune cell migration and angiogenic pathways. Effect of combining with systemic immunosuppression is unknown; potential for altered immune regulation.

No published study has given TB-500 itself to people, and FDA's July 2026 briefing found no human exposure data for it by any route. Two published phase 1 trials gave the full 43-amino-acid thymosin beta-4 intravenously instead. Ruff 2010 enrolled 40 healthy volunteers [5]; a 2021 Chinese study enrolled 54 single-dose and 30 multiple-dose volunteers [2]. Safety data for the fragment comes almost entirely from community self-reports. Injection site reactions are the most frequently reported problem. Redness, swelling, and tenderness at the injection site appear in a large percentage of users. Rotating between abdomen and thigh reduces local accumulation. Blistering, progressive swelling, or spreading warmth beyond the injection site is abnormal and requires stopping immediately. Fatigue and lethargy during the loading phase (weeks 1 to 2) rank second. Community reports describe this as the most common early side effect at doses of 4 to 5 mg per week. It usually resolves by week 3 without dose adjustment. If fatigue is debilitating, stepping down to 2 mg twice weekly is the standard community recommendation. Headache during loading is common and typically follows the same resolution pattern as fatigue. Nausea is less frequent. Rare but serious reactions include fever above 100.4 degrees F, injection site blistering, skin rash, hives, and muscle aches. Any of these require stopping the protocol and seeking medical evaluation. The unresolved long-term concern is oncogenic risk. TB-500 is pro-angiogenic. It promotes new blood vessel formation. In the presence of occult tumor tissue, this mechanism could theoretically support vascularization and tumor growth. Active cancer or personal cancer history is an absolute contraindication at any dose. Baseline age-appropriate cancer screening (PSA, mammogram, colonoscopy as applicable) is recommended before starting, particularly for anyone over 40. TB-500 is WADA prohibited (S2: Growth Factors) in and out of competition. A 4-year ban was issued in 2024 for documented use. DoD personnel face the same restriction. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: no safety data exists. Do not use.
Common Issues & Solutions

No results after 3–4 weeks: Most common cause is skipping the loading phase. Single weekly injections at maintenance dose from the start are insufficient: TB-500 requires 2×/week loading to establish adequate tissue-level concentrations. Restart with a proper 6-week loading phase.

Fatigue and lethargy during loading: Expected in weeks 1–2 at 4–5 mg/week+. Usually self-resolves by week 3. If debilitating, reduce to 2 mg 2×/week and reassess. Do not abandon the loading phase for mild fatigue: this is the most common cause of undertreatment.

Continuing injurious activity during protocol: The most cited reason for poor healing outcomes in community reports. TB-500 accelerates tissue repair but does not protect against re-injury from continued loading of the damaged structure. Relative rest of the injured tissue is strongly recommended.

Injection site reactions: Mild redness and tenderness are expected. Rotating sites (abdomen, thigh, alternating sides) minimizes local accumulation. Blistering, progressive swelling, spreading redness, or warmth extending beyond the injection site warrants stopping and medical evaluation for infection.

Sourcing and quality concerns: TB-500 is listed as withdrawn from FDA Category 2 (FDA page current as of April 22, 2026), but no FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list, so compounding pharmacies cannot use it today (PCAC discussed it July 23, 2026). All available supply is gray-market research-grade product with no regulatory quality assurance. Endotoxin contamination, peptide mislabeling, and significant underdosing are documented community concerns. Price does not measure purity. Only an independent lab test of a specific batch, covering HPLC purity and endotoxin, shows what a vial actually holds.

faqs.q: What is the recommended TB-500 dosage?
faqs.a: Loading phase: 2,000-2,500 mcg subcutaneous, twice per week for 4-6 weeks. Maintenance: 1,000-2,000 mcg once weekly (community reports). The loading phase front-loads systemic thymosin beta-4 levels. Some community protocols run 5,000 mcg twice weekly for acute injuries.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of TB-500?
faqs.a: Community reports from hundreds of users most commonly mention temporary lethargy, mild headache, and a "healing flare" (temporary increase in pain or inflammation at the injury site during weeks 1-2). This flare typically resolves by week 3 and may indicate increased repair activity. No formal human safety data exists for the fragment itself.

TB-500 is a synthetic version of the active region (amino acids 17-23) of thymosin beta-4. It promotes actin polymerization, which allows cells to migrate toward damaged tissue. The peptide also upregulates anti-inflammatory cytokines and promotes new blood vessel formation. Its 7-10 day functional activity window explains why less frequent dosing is effective.

faqs.q: How long does TB-500 take to work?
faqs.a: Most users report noticeable improvement in soft tissue injuries by weeks 2-3 of the loading phase. Tendon and ligament injuries may take 4-8 weeks to show clear progress. The healing timeline depends heavily on injury severity, location, and whether you're combining TB-500 with BPC-157 or other peptides.

TB-500 was on the FDA Category 2 bulk drug substance list from 2024 until its nominators withdrew it; FDA's Category 2 page (current as of April 22, 2026) lists it as withdrawn. PCAC discussed it on July 23, 2026. No FDA rule has added it to the 503A bulks list, so compounding pharmacies cannot use it today.
TB-500 typically comes in 2mg or 5mg or 10mg vials. Add 1mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of TB-500?
faqs.a: The half-life of TB-500 is ~5 hours (estimated, never measured in humans). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.
